question_text:
(a) It was pointed out that the temperature sensitivity of conductivity in semiconductors makes them superior to traditional thermocouples for certain high-precision temperature measurements. Such devices are referred to as thermistors. As a simple example, consider a wire 0.5 mm in diameter $\times 10 \mathrm{~mm}$ long made of intrinsic silicon. If the resistance of the wire can be measured to within $10^{-3} \Omega$, calculate the temperature sensitivity of this device at 300 K . (Hint: The very small differences here may make you want to develop an expression for $d \sigma / d T$.) (b) Repeat the calculation for an intrinsic germanium wire of the same dimensions. (c) For comparison with the temperature sensitivity of a metallic conductor, repeat the calculation for a copper (annealed standard) wire of the same dimensions. (The necessary data for this case can be found in Table.) Give your answer as a tuple: (temperature_sensitivity_silicon, temperature_sensitivity_germanium, temperature_sensitivity_copper).
(Table:
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
\hline \multicolumn{3}{|l|}{Resistivities and Temperature Coefficients of Resistivity for Some Metallic Conductors} \\
\hline Material & Resistivity at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \rho_{\mathrm{rt}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \mathrm{m})$ & Temperature coefficient of resistivity at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \alpha\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}^{-1}\right)$ \\
\hline Aluminum (annealed) & $28.28 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.0039 \\
\hline Copper (annealed standard) & $17.24 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.00393 \\
\hline Gold & $24.4 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.0034 \\
\hline Iron (99.99 + \% ) & $97.1 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.00651 \\
\hline Lead (99.73 + \% ) & $206.48 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.00336 \\
\hline Magnesium (99.80\%) & $44.6 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.01784 \\
\hline Mercury & $958 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.00089 \\
\hline Nickel (99.95\% + Co) & $68.4 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.0069 \\
\hline Nichrome (66\% Ni + Cr and Fe ) & $1,000 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.0004 \\
\hline Platinum (99.99\%) & $106 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.003923 \\
\hline Silver (99.78\%) & $15.9 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.0041 \\
\hline Steel (wire) & $107-175 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.006-0.0036 \\
\hline Tungsten & $55.1 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.0045 \\
\hline Zinc & $59.16 \times 10^{-9}$ & 0.00419 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
)The units of each required answer are (K, K, K), respectively.
response:
## Reasoning

**Setup.** The wire has $d=0.5\text{ mm}$, $L=10\text{ mm}$, so $A=\pi(0.25\times10^{-3})^2=1.963\times10^{-7}\text{ m}^2$ and $L/A=5.093\times10^{4}\text{ m}^{-1}$. Resistance measurable to $\Delta R=10^{-3}\,\Omega$. The temperature sensitivity (smallest detectable $\Delta T$) is

$$\Delta T=\frac{\Delta R}{|dR/dT|}.$$

**Semiconductors.** For an intrinsic semiconductor $\sigma = n_i e(\mu_e+\mu_h)\propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right)$, so

$$\frac{1}{\sigma}\frac{d\sigma}{dT}=\frac{E_g}{2kT^2}, \qquad \left|\frac{dR}{dT}\right|=R\,\frac{E_g}{2kT^2}, \qquad R=\frac{L}{\sigma A}.$$

Using standard 300 K data:
- **Si:** $E_g=1.107$ eV, $n_i=1.5\times10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, $\mu_e=0.135$, $\mu_h=0.048$ m²/V·s → $\sigma=4.40\times10^{-4}$ (Ω·m)$^{-1}$, $R=1.16\times10^{8}$ Ω, $E_g/2kT^2=0.0714$/K → $\Delta T=1.21\times10^{-10}$ K.
- **Ge:** $E_g=0.67$ eV, $n_i=2.4\times10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, $\mu_e=0.39$, $\mu_h=0.19$ m²/V·s → $\sigma=2.23$ (Ω·m)$^{-1}$, $R=2.28\times10^{4}$ Ω, $E_g/2kT^2=0.0432$/K → $\Delta T=1.01\times10^{-6}$ K.

**Copper.** Linear law $\rho=\rho_{20}[1+\alpha(T-20)]$ gives $d\rho/dT=\rho_{20}\alpha$. With $\rho_{20}=1.724\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m, $\alpha=0.00393$/°C:

$$\left|\frac{dR}{dT}\right|=\frac{L}{A}\rho_{20}\alpha=3.45\times10^{-6}\,\Omega/\text{K} \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta T=\frac{10^{-3}}{3.45\times10^{-6}}\approx 2.90\times10^{2}\text{ K}.$$

The result illustrates the thermistor advantage: intrinsic Si is ~12 orders of magnitude more temperature-sensitive than copper.

$$\boxed{\left(1.21\times10^{-10},\ 1.01\times10^{-6},\ 2.90\times10^{2}\right)}$$
